name: Sleep on your back (anti-wrinkle)

lead: Sleeping on your back keeps your face off the pillow, so the skin isn't compressed and folded night after night. People do it to avoid sleep lines and keep the face smoother over time.

Appearance communities promote it, and encyclopedic sources list habitual sleeping position among factors in skin wrinkles alongside aging, sun damage and facial expressions. The support cited is general educational material; no trial of sleep position and wrinkles was found.

paras: People train themselves to sleep supine, sometimes using pillows to hold the position, and often pair it with a silk pillowcase or a thin pillow. Visible changes are judged over months.
Back sleeping is associated with more sleep apnea, reflux and sleep paralysis in some people, so those prone to these may do better on their side.

web.title: Researchers review wrinkles occurring through facial compression during sleep - Healio

angle.text: Sleeping face-up keeps the skin from being folded against a pillow night after night, aiming to prevent sleep lines. Sleeping position is listed among wrinkle factors in reference sources, though no trial has tested the habit.

lead: Sleeping on the back is promoted in skincare and looksmaxxing circles as a free way to avoid 'sleep lines' and one-sided facial compression. The idea is that a face lying flat is not pressed into a pillow for hours each night, so skin is not folded or pushed in the same place repeatedly.[1][2]

The idea has a published basis in plastic surgery and dermatology. A 1999 Dermatologic Surgery paper by Fulton and Gaminchi described 'sleep lines' as creases accentuated by pillow contact and linked to attachments of the underlying superficial musculoaponeurotic system, and listed a change of sleeping position among the options for treatment [3]. A 2016 literature review in Aesthetic Surgery Journal by Anson, Kane and Lambros argued that facial tissue is pushed, pulled and compressed during side or stomach sleeping, that sleep wrinkles differ from expression wrinkles in cause, location and direction, and that avoiding facial distortion, for example by back sleeping, is the reliable way to minimise them [2][3]. The authors acknowledged that changing sleep habits is difficult and called for more study [2].

Wikipedia lists habitual sleeping position among factors contributing to skin wrinkles, alongside aging, sun damage and facial expressions.[1] Back sleeping also has health associations, including more positional sleep apnea and reflux in some people.[4] On looksmax.org, members debate whether side sleeping changes facial symmetry or wrinkles and how to learn to sleep supine.[5][6]
infobox: Fewer sleep lines and less one-sided compression
Anson, Kane and Lambros, Aesthetic Surgery Journal, 2016[3]; Fulton and Gaminchi, Dermatologic Surgery, 1999[3]

paras: The practice involves sleeping supine, sometimes with a pillow arrangement to keep the face off the bed. The Wikipedia article on wrinkles names habitual sleeping position as a contributing factor and points to a dermatology educational page.[1]

Healio's report on the 2016 review says the authors described sleep wrinkles as forming where skin buckles under external pressure, with habitual sleep patterns able to reinforce expression lines, and noted that specialty pillows designed to reduce facial distortion exist.[2]

Practitioners describe a few variations: sleeping fully supine on a flat or moderately raised pillow, using a pillow or rolled towel on each side to hold the body in place, and using a pillow with cut-outs or a shape intended to keep the face from being compressed.[2][6] Healio notes that specialty pillows designed to reduce facial distortion during sleep exist.[2]

Wikipedia describes wrinkles through a misrepair-accumulation theory in which repeated stretching and compression damage skin fibres, imperfect repair leaves skin looser and stiffer, and small permanent folds form; habitual sleeping positions are listed among contributors, alongside glycation, sun damage, smoking and habitual facial expressions.[1]

Anson and colleagues distinguish sleep wrinkles from expression wrinkles, saying they differ in mechanism of origin, location and direction, are less predictable, and tend to form where skin buckles under external pressure.[2] The authors also suggest that sleep patterns can reinforce expression lines over time.[2] Lead author Goesel Anson, a plastic surgeon in Las Vegas, was quoted by Healio as saying "A wrinkle is not just a wrinkle!" and that facial distortion during sleep deserves further study.[2]

Fulton and Gaminchi, writing in 1999, credited Dr. Samuel Stegman with describing 'sleep creases' in 1987. They reported that the position of sleep lines correlated with the location of underlying SMAS attachments or aberrant scar tissue, described a pillow test and hand test that accentuate the lines, and noted that treatment could involve a change of sleeping position, subcision of the attachments or skin resurfacing.[3]

The 2016 review examined how wrinkles develop from intrinsic and extrinsic influences, concluding that shear, compression and tension forces act on facial tissue during side or stomach sleeping, and that these forces may contribute to facial aging because of the many hours spent asleep.[2] The lead author disclosed a partnership with a company selling a sleep-wrinkle pillow, and the review is a literature analysis rather than a trial.[2]

The abstract of the 2016 review frames the idea that sleep compression may contribute to facial skin expansion as a possibility to explore rather than an established result.[3] Healio quoted the authors as concluding that the only reliable way to minimise sleep wrinkles is to avoid facial distortion, and reported that lead author Anson also disclosed an honorarium from and advisory-board role with Allergan.[2]

A looksmax.org thread on side versus back sleeping states that side sleeping contributes at most slightly to asymmetry, that only a few studies suggest it might lead to wrinkles or droopier eyelids over time, and that bone structure is not meaningfully changed by sleeping on one side.[5]

Supine sleeping is the second most common adult position after side sleeping, according to Wikipedia, and lateral preference rises with age and body mass.[4] Positional obstructive sleep apnea, which the article says accounts for 56 to 75 percent of regular obstructive sleep apnea patients, is the main concern with supine sleep, because gravity can pull the tongue into the airway.[4] Lying flat soon after eating can cause reflux, and supine sleep is linked to more frequent sleep paralysis.[4] Side sleeping is the most common adult position; right-side sleeping causes more nighttime reflux than left-side, and animal studies link lateral sleep to higher glymphatic activity.[4] The article says nothing about wrinkles or facial effects of any position.[4]

Forum members share methods for learning to sleep supine, including pillow arrangements and, in one looksmax.org thread, a hammock, which drew replies about spinal support.[6] An Ask HN thread in 2018 asked how to learn to sleep on the back and drew 75 comments, with posters comparing approaches to staying in position.[7] The 2016 review's authors themselves noted that changing sleep habits deliberately is difficult.[2]

Back sleeping is discussed in skincare circles as a free habit that targets one component of facial aging, and in looksmaxxing threads as a question of facial symmetry as well as lines. Members debate whether side sleeping changes symmetry or contributes to wrinkles or droopier eyelids over time, with one thread stating that any asymmetry effect is slight and that bone structure is not meaningfully changed.[5] The interest in back sleeping extends beyond appearance communities to people seeking comfort or health benefits.[7]

sections.h: Other approaches to sleep lines and wrinkles
paras: Wikipedia lists retinoids, hyaluronic acid products, dermal fillers, botulinum toxin and laser resurfacing as treatments for established wrinkles, and sun avoidance as prevention.[1] Back sleeping is discussed as a free habit that targets the sleep-line component specifically, alongside these treatments rather than in place of them.

No controlled trial comparing sleeping positions with wrinkle formation has been published. The research that exists is descriptive: a 1999 clinical and anatomical description of sleep lines and their link to SMAS attachments, and a 2016 literature review of the compression, shear and tension forces on the face during side or prone sleep.[3][3] The 2016 review is not a trial, and its lead author disclosed a partnership with a company that sells a sleep-wrinkle pillow.[2] A 2026 study in Anais Brasileiros de Dermatologia examined frontal wrinkles in older adults and the association of sleep lines with sleep quality.[3]

lore.intro: Back sleeping appears in skincare and looksmaxxing discussion as a free anti-aging habit, alongside debate about side sleeping and asymmetry.[5][6]

claims.claim: Side and stomach sleeping cause lasting sleep wrinkles
